segments.text: Ternary relationships: when one fact needs three entities at once.
Most relationships link two entities. But some facts need three at the same time.
Mike takes Physics with Jones. Drop any one of the three, and the fact is no longer complete.
So we draw one diamond with three lines: a ternary relationship. With four entities, it would be quaternary.
To read its cardinalities, fix the other two entities, then count.
For one student and one course, how many instructors? Exactly one. So we write one, one at Instructor.
For one course and one instructor, how many students? One or more: one, N at Student.
Course works the same way. Read together, the maxima give the ratio: M to N to one.
A ternary ratio has one of four shapes: one one one, one one N, one M N, or M N P.
A one at an end means the other entities decide it, so together they form the key.
Here, student and course identify each row.
Now look at the pairs inside it. Mike goes with two courses; Physics goes with two instructors.
Two by two, the entities are many to many. A rule about a pair, like one instructor per course, must be stated on its own.
Could three binary relationships replace the ternary? Let's try.
Split the three facts into pairs: student and course, course and instructor, student and instructor.
Now join the pairs back. Mike, Physics, Song: every pair exists, so the row appears.
But Mike never took Physics with Song. The split invented a fact, so keep the ternary.
In the logical model, a ternary becomes one table, with a foreign key to each entity.
Its primary key is made of the ends with max N: student and course.
Practise it in the E R concepts section of the course site.
